item.title: Guerra Interpolation and Optimal Transport: Kantorovich Bounds, Brenier Maps and the Replicon
item.dc:creator: Elena Agliari, Adriano Barra, Andrea Ladiana, Andrea Lepre, Diego Pallara
item.description:
All numbered theorems, propositions and lemmas are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib in the GuerraHJ library: 7,891 lines, 519 results, no sorry.
Since Guerra's work, mean-field spin glasses have been studied through Hamilton–Jacobi equations. Here, using the Curie–Weiss and the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick models as prototypical examples, we show that his celebrated interpolation method is itself an optimal transport computation. After a linear change of variables the finite-$N$ pressure becomes an action $u$ with $\partial_t u = -A/2$ and $\partial_x u = -B$, where $B^2 \le A$, so $u$ is a classical subsolution of $\partial_t u+\frac12(\partial_x u)^2 \le 0$. Integrating along a straight segment gives Guerra's sum rule, and dropping its remainder makes $u(0,\cdot)$ and $u(t,\cdot)$ an admissible pair for the dual Kantorovich problem with quadratic cost. For the Curie–Weiss model and $t > 0$, $T_t(y) = y-t\tanh y$ is an optimal transport map from every source with finite first moment if and only if $t \le 1$, and the Kantorovich potentials are the limiting pressures. For the replica-symmetric Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model, the cavity map is injective on the physical half-line and the curvature of its Brenier potential is the longitudinal eigenvalue, which exceeds the replicon eigenvalue $Λ_{\mathrm{AT}}$: transport of Dirac masses does not detect the de Almeida–Thouless line. The replicon appears along the $\mathcal{W}_2$ geodesic that splits a Dirac mass into two atoms, as the second variation of a second-order surrogate of the two-atom Parisi functional. From a Dirac initial datum, Guerra's $K$-step bound takes Hopf–Lax form, and the Parisi formula becomes a Hopf–Lax formula over atomic measures. With a $\mathcal{W}_1$-Lipschitz bound for its initial datum, proved by comparing Cole–Hopf layers, we let $K\to\infty$ and recover at Dirac data the Hopf–Lax form of the Parisi formula due to Mourrat and to Mourrat and Panchenko, with a rate for equal-mass approximations.

item.title: A narrow band method for non-causal discretizations of anisotropic eikonal equations, with adaptive width, sub-and super-solution construction, and quasi-linear complexity
item.dc:creator: Jean-Marie Mirebeau, Yanis Mouheb
item.description:
All lemmas, propositions and theorems on the narrow band method were formalized in Lean with Claude AI assistance, marked Lean✓ throughout.
We describe a narrow band method for numerically solving anisotropic eikonal equations, and more generally static first order Hamilton-Jacobi equations with possibly non-convex Hamiltonians, discretized using standard schemes (semi-Lagrangian, upwind-differences, Lax-Friedrichs). The causality property is not needed, in contrast with the fast marching method. The proposed approach simultaneously builds a numerical sub-solution u and super-solution u to the problem, and adapts the width of the narrow band based on their comparison. We prove that (1 + $ε$)u $\ge$ u at termination, where $ε$ > 0 is any given tolerance parameter, and that the worst case complexity is O(N | ln $ε$| ln(N/$ε$)), where N denotes the number of discretization points, and the underlying constant is explicit in terms of those associated with the scheme properties. Numerical experiments illustrate our results.

item.title: Compiling Matrix Formulas to Quantum Block Encodings
item.dc:creator: Daksh Shami, Charles Yuan
item.description:
The authors use Lean 4 to mechanize proofs that each of MARBLE's algebraic rewrite rules preserves matrix semantics and well-formedness of the symbolic form.
Realizing the promise of quantum applications such as chemistry or fluid dynamics requires building quantum circuits that efficiently encode and manipulate exponentially large matrices. This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup. In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It analyzes costs of possible representations, notably the subnormalization term that dominates time complexity. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms. When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.

item.title: Semistable 1-Motives: Monodromy, Explicit Periods, and Local Duality
item.dc:creator: Mohammadreza Mohajer
item.description:
Selected algebraic results and proofs were formalized and checked in Lean 4, with nine checks in a companion GitHub repository.
Let $K/\mathbf Q_p$ be unramified, with $p>2$. For a $1$-motive with constant lattice, split torus, and good abelian quotient, we compute the semistable extension complex from toric valuations and formal-group logarithms. A canonical monodromy boundary exists for every semistable representation; it detects splitting over crystalline periods and the increase in monodromy rank. For the stated $1$-motives, this boundary and the unramified quotient recover the restricted local Tate pairing, with exponential radicals. Nonsplit elliptic examples, Raynaud uniformization, and a height-one positive-period bound explain the geometric range. For toric motives we construct actual periods, convergent Robba bases, and integral action matrices. A toric basis family has perfect projective/trace-zero matrix duality, including its exact integral defect. An explicit residue-zero solution operator constructs every dual Herr class. Applied componentwise, the same operator gives relative full dual lifts for general constant-lattice $1$-motives once their coefficient sequence is specified. Finally, finite-base coefficient traces realize division-tower Iwasawa cohomology for any Tate lattice, and the period cup pairing equals the arithmetic group-ring pairing.

item.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
item.dc:creator: You-Lin Chen, Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaojing Yu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu
item.description:
The paper's statistical guarantees are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib measure theory. The proofs were AI-generated, and Comparator checks that the Lean claims match the paper's statements.
Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

item.title: Higher-order estimates for $p$-harmonic functions in the plane
item.dc:creator: Juan J. Manfredi, Aelson Sobral, Eduardo V. Teixeira, José Miguel Urbano
item.description:
Theorem 1.1, the higher-order estimates for planar p-harmonic functions, was formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib using AI tools; the code is published on GitHub.
Closing a longstanding gap in the theory, we establish uniform interior $C^{k,β}$ estimates for planar $p$-harmonic functions with $1<p<2$. These estimates hold for every integer $k\ge2$ and every $0<β<1$ such that $k+β<s(p)$, where $s(p)$ is the optimal regularity order identified by Iwaniec and Manfredi. As consequences, we obtain decay estimates at critical points, a Liouville theorem with optimal growth exponent, and uniform higher-order estimates for the flux of planar $q$-harmonic functions with $q>2$.

item.title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
item.dc:creator: Xueying Qin, Marco Peressotti, Fabrizio Montesi
item.description:
The entire choreographic calculus Nyarlathotep, including EPP soundness, completeness, communication safety and deadlock freedom, is mechanised in about 20,000 lines of Lean 4 using CSLib.
Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

item.title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
item.dc:creator: Biswa Sengupta, Jinhua Wang, Léo Maxime Brunswic
item.description:
Every theorem and proposition about Muon's update, Newton–Schulz iteration, block polar factors and second-order criteria is proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $σ^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically principled changes that do not act on the measured miscalibration, namely exact polar factors, steepest-descent input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.

item.title: Only the disk: topological obstructions for warped AdS$_6\times S^2$ in Type IIB
item.dc:creator: Nakwoo Kim
item.description:
Counting steps of the main theorems, pointwise identities and a boundary rotation bound were formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib; files ship as ancillary files.
Supersymmetric AdS$_6\times S^2$ solutions of Type IIB supergravity are warped products over a Riemann surface $Σ$. They are determined by two holomorphic differentials on $Σ$, with five-branes at poles on its boundary. We derive restrictions on the genus and the number of boundary components of $Σ$. Without seven-branes or orientifolds, the differentials are taken to be single-valued on $Σ$. Regularity implies that the number of interior zeros of one differential equals the total rotation of the phase of the ratio of the two differentials along the boundary. It also bounds this rotation on each boundary component by the number of poles on that component. Combined with the known count of zeros on the double of $Σ$, these two statements force $Σ$ to be a disk. With mutually local seven-branes and orientifolds as interior punctures, the same conclusion follows under additional assumptions on the global structure of the differentials and on their behavior at the punctures. The disk then admits at most one orientifold puncture. On a disk without punctures, the bound applied between successive poles also recovers the known cyclic ordering of the five-brane charges along the boundary.

item.title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
item.dc:creator: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg, Ke Sun, Hartmut Haeffner
item.description:
Implements a QCCD trapped-ion compiler in Lean 4 and proves an end-to-end theorem that compiled code preserves program behavior and satisfies the hardware rules given as inputs.
Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

item.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
item.dc:creator: Bowen Zhu, Jian Wu
item.description:
Imports a Lean 4 relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell formalization and adds eleven new Lean modules proving exterior-field, Poynting-balance, Yee-invariance and mode-rank bounds used to certify PIC solvers.
AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from OpenAI's Lean 4 relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.

item.title: Existence of SRB measures for some Rössler systems
item.dc:creator: Théophile Caby
item.description:
The analytic homoclinic-tangency criterion and an associated Taylor bound are formalised and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the numerical part is not.
We prove that for the Rössler system $\dot x=-(y+z)$, $\dot y=x+ay$, $\dot z=b+z(x-c)$ with $a=b=0.2$, the set of parameters $c$ within $6\cdot10^{-5}$ of the classical value $c=5.7$ for which the flow has a Hénon-like strange attractor supporting a Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measure has positive Lebesgue measure. The key step, proved with computer assistance, is that at a parameter localised in an explicit interval within $5.5\cdot10^{-5}$ of $5.7$ the period-one saddle of the Poincaré map has a quadratic homoclinic tangency that unfolds generically; the conclusion then follows from the theorems of Mora–Viana, Benedicks–Young and Benedicks–Viana. The same method gives two further such tangencies near $5.7$ and one at the band-merging parameter $c\approx4.507$. The proof reduces the generic-tangency conditions to finitely many inequalities, through explicit $C^2$ graph-transform bounds for the local invariant manifolds of a Poincaré map whose area contraction is of order $10^{-11}$–$10^{-14}$, and a scalar tangency function. The inequalities are checked with interval arithmetic in CAPD and re-checked with an independent implementation based on the Kv library; the analytic tangency criterion is formalised in Lean 4. Whether an SRB measure exists at $c=5.7$ itself remains open.

item.title: Delaunay Combinatorics of the Moduli and Teichmüller Space of Closed Genus-Two Riemann Surfaces
item.dc:creator: Armando Rodado Amaris
item.description:
The finite combinatorial classification of Delaunay graph types, their automorphism groups and the flip orbit are verified in Lean 4 using native_decide.
Every closed Riemann surface of genus two is hyperelliptic, so it is determined by six branch points on the sphere, which become cone points of angle pi in the quotient orbifold metric. The Delaunay decomposition of these cone points, dual to the Voronoi diagram of the Weierstrass points, gives a trivalent graph with eight vertices, twelve edges and six faces. We classify these graphs. When the dual triangulation is simple there are exactly two types, dual to the octahedron and to a stacked triangulation, with orientation-preserving automorphism groups of orders 24 and 2, and we determine the Whitehead-move (diagonal-flip) orbit connecting them. Allowing bigons, the orbit closes at exactly twenty types. Iterated edge contraction from the two simple types gives a seven-level hierarchy of 2, 6, 22, 32, 22, 5 and 1 types, ending at two vertices joined by six parallel edges; closing under both contraction and expansion gives all 280 maps on the sphere with six vertices and no vertex of degree one. The rank of the linear cone-angle system of each type equals the real dimension 6 of the Teichmüller space. We realize both simple types by explicit hyperbolic cone spheres, in closed form for the octahedral type, build the corresponding genus-two surfaces by cutting and doubling, and show that the boundary x_e = 0 of the angle system is exactly the concyclicity of four branch points. The classification, the automorphism groups and the flip orbit are formally verified in Lean 4, and every enumeration is reproduced by an independent program, which also determines which types are realized by Delaunay decompositions.

item.title: New lower bounds for even and odd values of the partition function
item.dc:creator: Liuquan Wang
item.description:
The paper's lower bounds for the parity counts of the partition function were formally verified in Lean by AxiomProver; the files are in a public repository.
Let $N_{\mathrm{odd}}(X)$ and $N_{\mathrm{even}}(X)$ denote the numbers of integers $0\leq n\leq X$ for which the ordinary partition function $p(n)$ is odd and even, respectively. The Parkin–Shanks conjecture predicts that $N_{\mathrm{odd}}(X)$ and $N_{\mathrm{even}}(X)$ are both asymptotic to $X/2$. Bellaïche and Nicolas proved that $N_{\mathrm{even}}(X)\gg \sqrt{X} \log \log X$, while Zheng, building on work of Ono and Swaminathan, recently proved that $N_{\mathrm{odd}}(X)\gg \sqrt{X}$. We improve both bounds simultaneously by proving $\min\{N_{\mathrm{odd}}(X), N_{\mathrm{even}}(X)\}\gg X^{3/4}/(\log X \log \log X)$. These results have been verified formally in Lean by AxiomProver.

item.title: Combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication in $n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})}$ Time
item.dc:creator: Piaoyang Cui, Yiming Liu, David P. Woodruff
item.description:
Main theorems on combinatorial BMM and triangle detection are machine-checked in Lean 4 with zero sorries, using a cost-accounting monad for running time.
For over fifty years, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication (BMM) and triangle detection saved only polylogarithmic factors over cubic time. At STOC 2024, Abboud, Fischer, Kelley, Lovett, and Meka broke this barrier with a deterministic $O(n^3 / 2^{Ω((\log n)^{1/7})})$-time algorithm, and asked whether $n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time is achievable. We answer this question in the affirmative, giving deterministic combinatorial algorithms for both BMM and triangle detection running in $O(n^3 / 2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log n})})$ time. Following Abboud et al., we decompose $(A,B)$ into pairs of submatrices $(A_k,B_k)$, called pieces, each of which is either sparse or pseudorandom in a sense that forces $A_k\star B_k$ to be nearly all-ones on its vertex sets. Whereas their decomposition produces $2^{O(d^7)}$ pieces at regularity parameter $d$, we obtain $2^{O(d^2)}$ pieces, directly improving the runtime exponent from $(\log n)^{1/7}$ to $\sqrt{\log n}$. Prior work found pseudorandom pieces by repeatedly restricting to denser submatrices, paying worst-case vertex losses at each step that compounded across nested recursion levels, together with an expensive derandomization step. We eliminate the extra powers of $d$ by matching the vertex loss at each step to the size of its density jump so losses telescope across scales, derandomizing witness search via $L_d$-norm estimation so the sampler length stays $2^{O(d)}$, and bounding overlap across the recursion with a fractional density-weighted volume budget rather than raw submatrix volume.

item.title: Linearize or Discretize First? Error Estimates under Mesh-Uniform Regularity and Exponential Stability for the KdV Equation with Boundary Dissipation
item.dc:creator: Kangsheng Liu
item.description:
Theorems 4.1–4.4 on the ordering error were checked in Lean 4 under certain premises, using AI tools following an author-designed procedure.
We study the Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation, and its spatial semidiscretization by a weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin method. A small nonlinear wave can be approximated by a linear discrete simulation in two orders: linearize first and then discretize, or discretize first and then linearize. Both orders lead to the same total error. They divide this error differently between linearization and discretization. The difference of the two divisions is what we call the ordering error. We show that it is quadratic in the size of the initial datum and carries a positive power of the mesh size, for all time. It can be used to assess the effect of a coarse-mesh correction for nonlinear problems. For the continuous problem, the solution map is analytic, and the semigroup of the linearized equation has Crandall-Pazy regularity with the exact index 3/2. For the weighted scheme, the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit exponential stability, Kato smoothing and Crandall-Pazy regularity, with bounds uniform in the mesh size. The nonlinear solution maps are analytic, also uniformly in the mesh size. These properties give error estimates in which the error and the datum are measured in the same norm: in the energy norm, in $H_0^1$ and in $H^2$. On every interval $[t_0,\infty)$, $t_0>0$, same-norm convergence holds uniformly on balls at algebraic rates. The ordering error is of order $h^{1/6}$ times the square of the energy norm of the datum, uniformly for all $t\ge0$.

item.title: Calibrated for Which Policy? Conformal Uncertainty for Fixed World Models Under Intervention
item.dc:creator: Ayush Mittal, Dhruv Gupta
item.description:
Finite-support versions of the posterior-to-ratio identity, classifier-regret bound, policy-shift factorization, and coverage composition are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Changing a deployment policy can invalidate a world model's uncertainty while leaving the physical transition mechanism and predictor unchanged. For one-step prediction, if source and target laws share the conditional mechanism $P(Y|X)=Q(Y|X)$, then the intervention is identified by the pre-outcome change of measure $w(X)=dQ_X/dP_X$. For policy-controlled dynamics this ratio factors into state-occupancy and action-propensity terms. Weighted conformal calibration transports marginal coverage to the target law; with an estimated ratio $\hat w$, $P_Q\{Y \in C_{\hat w}(X)\} \ge 1-α-TV(Q,\hat Q) \ge 1-α-E_P|w-\hat w|$. Population log-loss regret for a source-versus-target domain classifier bounds the same ratio error. If $h$ is its clipped target posterior, $ρ$ is the target-domain prior, and $Δ(h)$ is population log-loss regret, then $E_P|w-\hat w_h| \le (1/(ργ))\sqrt{Δ(h)/2}$. An exact cancellation improves the dependence from a generic odds-map bound of order $γ^{-2}$ to $(ργ)^{-1}$. Our experiments use a released DINO-feature world model and physical Franka trajectories. Under the strongest controlled state-action shift, ordinary 90% conformal sets cover 55.0%, whereas oracle and learned-ratio calibration cover 91.0% and 90.9%. The learned surrogate remains within 0.9% total variation of the target law. Calibration is relative to the deployment law: the model can remain fixed while calibration follows the intervention. We machine-check in Lean 4 the finite-support algebraic and causal identities used in the classifier-regret argument, including its coverage-composition step.

item.title: Webs and exponentially large mu-coefficients
item.dc:creator: Tom Goertzen, Abel Lacabanne, Daniel Tubbenhauer, Pedro Vaz
item.description:
Lean formalization verifies the local tensor and web diagram calculations, the lattice induction, and the two-state readout for every block count; code is in a public repository.
Using webs, we prove that Kazhdan-Lusztig mu-coefficients for symmetric groups grow at least exponentially with the rank, already for pairs labeled by a three-row rectangle.

item.title: Beyond Brown's radial tests: admissibility, parabolicity, and a doubling-Poincaré prior that neither test decides
item.dc:creator: Oleg Roshka
item.description:
Part of the potential-theoretic results is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib: 37 modules and 655 theorems, with cited results carried as named hypotheses.
For the estimation of a normal mean in $\mathbb{R}^m$ under quadratic loss, Brown (1971) proved that a generalized Bayes estimator $δ_F$ with bounded drift is admissible if and only if a diffusion attached to the marginal $f^*$ of the prior $F$ is recurrent, and gave two radial tests: a sphere-average test for recurrence and a ray test for transience. He observed that both tests can be silent. We read his theory as the potential theory of the weighted Euclidean space $(\mathbb{R}^m,f^*\,dx)$ and ask what the modern theory of recurrence on weighted manifolds adds inside the zone where neither test applies. Three results. (A) If $f^*\,dx$ is doubling and supports a scale-invariant Poincaré inequality, the sphere test is already complete: recurrence, Brown's sphere test and the ball-volume test are equivalent, so geometric criteria can add decidable cases only on the inadmissible side. (B) They do add one. An explicit prior on $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose marginal is small along a lattice of circles at dyadic scales with spacing equal to the square root of the scale is doubling and Poincaré, silences both of Brown's tests, and is transient by the ball-volume test; its generalized Bayes estimator is inadmissible. (C) Outside the doubling-Poincaré class the zone is two-sided: similar circles placed on one surface per scale give an admissible estimator, decided by a flux bound along a non-spherical exhaustion, and a logarithmic product prior gives an inadmissible one, decided by product heat kernels. A comparison lemma shows that any positive weight with Lipschitz logarithm is, up to constants, the marginal of a prior, so that explicit weights may be used throughout.

item.title: Verification and Self-Improvement in Agentic AI: Foundations and Limits
item.dc:creator: Chien-Ping Lu
item.description:
Ancillary Lean 4/Mathlib project machine-checks bounded semantic replacement, an evaluator recurrence, and adaptive-selection error-budget propositions using Mathlib probability.
A self-improving agent can find accepted solutions more often without expanding the tasks its verification interface can accept. We extend task-relative verification with explicit support and transcript interfaces to distinguish search gains from changes in accepted-task coverage. A stage's native reach contains tasks accepted with default support; its closure frontier contains tasks accepted with any support the declared interface permits. A semantic containment criterion identifies the authority or exposure condition that every verified escape must violate, while guard-transfer invariance prevents a change of representation from being counted as a capability expansion. An executable Boolean-program repair agent makes the distinction concrete: over 36,864 paired runs, counterexample feedback reduces verifier calls without changing coverage, whereas an enforced permission change admits a new target with a proof excluding every old-interface program. Exact and uniformly gapped randomized verification share this account; independent majority amplification improves reliability while preserving the accepted language. Separate adaptive-selection contracts state what is additionally required to interpret a proposed successor's score as evidence of deployment improvement. Classical hierarchy results and finite audits provide supporting boundaries. The framework specifies the evidence needed to establish improved search, wider accepted capability, and reliable successor selection.

item.title: Two Answers on Heavy-Ball Dynamics
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Takáč
item.description:
The heavy-ball worst-case rate and convergence-threshold results are accompanied by formal proofs in Lean.
We determine the worst-case behavior of the heavy-ball method on smooth strongly convex functions, first for Polyak's quadratic-optimal parameters and then for arbitrary constant parameters. For Polyak's tuning, the exact dimension-uniform exponential rate is the largest growth factor of an interpolable mixture of rotating geometric sequences. Four algebraic families determine this rate at every condition number. Two frequencies suffice, and one function in dimension five attains the rate at every horizon up to constant factors. We recover the sharp convergence threshold $9+4\sqrt5$ of Badithela and Seiler. For general tunings, an exact linear feasibility criterion characterizes dimension-uniform linear convergence through the angle between the characteristic polynomials of the two extreme quadratics. This gives a continuous condition-number threshold and resolves the second heavy-ball riddle of Goujaud, Taylor and Dieuleveut. The regions between consecutive cycle tongues are Farey gaps, each containing convergent and divergent tunings. Regular portions of the threshold surface are analytic plateaus with fixed periodic frequency support. Every rational rotation number in a gap anchors a single-harmonic plateau; mixed-harmonic plateaus and an exact two-lag threshold point also occur. Along tongue edges, explicit multiplier inequalities and second-order expansions of competing Farey fans bound the transition from single-harmonic to mixed-harmonic extremals. The rate bounds and the extremal constructions follow from a common interpolation and separation argument that preserves initialization with zero momentum.

item.title: Rounded Clocks and Finite Precision: A Transfer Principle Between Continuous and Discrete Quantum Dynamics
item.dc:creator: Michael Jarret
item.description:
The definitions, theorems, and examples, including the comparison identity and the O(1/T) transfer theorem, are tagged with links to Lean formalizations.
I present a short approach to discretizing continuous unitary evolution in finite dimensions. For a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(s)$ with $s\in[0,1]$ and an integer $T\ge1$, let $U(T)$ be the evolution of $H(t/T)$ over time $T$, and let $W_T=e^{-iH((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-iH(0)}$ be the product of the unitaries generated by its samples. With a half-step phase at each end, $V(T)=e^{-iH(1)/2}W_Te^{iH(0)/2}$ is the evolution generated by $H(\lfloor t+1/2\rfloor/T)$, where $\lfloor t+1/2\rfloor$ is a rounded clock, time at finite precision. Whereas Duhamel's formula only bounds $\|V(T)-U(T)\|$ by a constant, I show that $\|V(T)-U(T)\|=O(1/T)$ in operator norm, with explicit constants, whenever $H'$ is Lipschitz and every sample has eigenvalue differences at most a fixed width below $2π$. The gain comes from cancellation within and between time steps. This general transfer theorem assumes neither adiabaticity nor a spectral gap, and any operator-norm bound for $U(T)$ transfers to $V(T)$ with an added $O(1/T)$. Nonetheless, discrete adiabatic theorems for $W_T$ follow from continuous ones, because the end phases commute with the spectral projectors of $H(0)$ and $H(1)$. For a product of samples of a $C^2$ unitary family, a continuously moving arc of fixed length $\vartheta$ that avoids the spectrum determines a Hermitian logarithm meeting the width condition, and the $O(1/T)$ bound has coefficients $O(\vartheta^{-3})$. In the easier direction, Duhamel's formula shows that rounding the clock to midpoints and truncating the entries of a regulated time-dependent Hamiltonian at a fixed binary place gives a product within $T$ times the error of the rounded, truncated Hamiltonian.

item.title: Square-Root Regret for Adversarial Multiplayer Bandits without Collision Information or Shared Randomness
item.dc:creator: Chenyu Gan
item.description:
The paper's mathematical results, excluding the computational complexity claims, are formalized in Lean, with a public repository.
We study cooperative multiplayer bandits with adversarial rewards and no collision information. In each of $T$ rounds, each of $m$ labeled players picks one of $K>m$ arms. A player alone on its arm receives that arm's reward in $[0,1]$; players who share an arm receive $0$. Each player observes only its own reward, so it cannot distinguish a collision from an arm with zero reward, and there is neither shared randomness nor a communication channel. Bubeck, Li, Peres and Sellke (2020) obtained regret $\widetilde O(KT^{3/4})$ for two players and $\widetilde O(mK^{3/2}T^{1-1/(2m)})$ for $m$ players, and conjectured that regret $Ω(T^{2/3})$ is unavoidable already for two players. We refute this conjecture. We give a strategy whose expected regret against every oblivious adversary is $O(m^{3/2}\sqrt{KT}\log^2(KmT))$, which is optimal in $K$ and $T$ up to logarithmic factors. Three ideas make this possible. (i) Bits are sent through deliberate collisions as random parity checks, and the regret spent while a message is delayed is charged to the number of arms with positive reward rather than to elapsed time: an adversary that jams the channel with zero rewards forfeits the regret it could inflict. (ii) An exponential-weights learner over sets of arms combines a frequently resampled coordinator arm with a follower assignment that changes only $O(\sqrt{mT/K})$ times in expectation; delayed updates are reconstructed exactly. (iii) We teach the followers a privately chosen row index in a fixed public table using reward observations alone, allowing them to coordinate without shared randomness. The bound holds simultaneously for all reward matrices, even ones chosen with knowledge of the table, and a random table works with probability $1-O(1/(KmT))$.

item.title: Large deviations of the spectral radius of iid subgaussian random matrices
item.dc:creator: Yi Han
item.description:
The paper's results on spectral-radius large deviations are formalized in Lean, with repositories released, including one for the upper-tail bounds.
We study large deviations of the spectral radius of $X_n=n^{-1/2}(ξ_{ij})_{i,j=1}^n$, where the entries are iid, centered, variance-one, and subgaussian, with zero pseudovariance in the complex case. We write $ρ(X_n)$ for its spectral radius, i.e. the largest modulus among its eigenvalues. For every fixed $r>1$, we prove $$ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\mathbb{P}\{ρ(X_n)>r\} \ge -\frac\beta2\bigl(r^2-1-2\log r\bigr), $$ where $β=1$ for real entries and $β=2$ for complex entries. We prove a matching upper bound for real symmetric laws with Gaussian-dominated even moments and for complex laws satisfying the sharp Gaussian Laplace-transform bound. These classes include discrete distributions. In the complex sharp class, we also identify the exponential rate for an eigenvalue to enter a fixed disk outside the unit disk. We then turn to lower deviations and establish a quadratic-speed bound. Under the additional assumption that the entry law $μ$ has a bounded density, we prove $$ \mathbb{P}\{ρ(X_n)\le r\}\le e^{-c_{μ,r}n^2} $$ for every fixed $0<r<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, where $c_{μ,r}>0$. For the matching upper-tail classes with a bounded density, these bounds give a full speed-$n$ large deviation principle, with the displayed upper-tail rate for $r\ge1$ and infinite rate for $r<1$. The upper-tail proof uses a change of measure that preserves the entry support and creates an outlying eigenvalue. The lower-tail proof develops a weighted comparison for adaptive orthonormal observations and applies it to Arnoldi residuals.

item.title: Computing distances in braid-move graphs, higher Bruhat orders, and oriented-matroid mutation graphs is NP-hard
item.dc:creator: Tilen Marc
item.description:
The main distance formulas, excess amplification and VC-equivalences are formally verified in core Lean 4, with a public repository and no unproved steps.
A wiring diagram is an arrangement of $m$ pseudolines, every two of which cross exactly once. Reading its crossings from left to right encodes it as a reduced word of the permutation $w_0\in S_m$ that reverses $1,\dots,m$, unique up to commutations, and a braid move $σ_iσ_{i+1}σ_i\leftrightarrowσ_{i+1}σ_iσ_{i+1}$ flips one of its triangles. We prove that deciding whether two wiring diagrams are within a given braid-move distance is NP-complete. Equivalently, deciding flip distance is NP-complete in the higher Bruhat order $B(m,2)$, for triangle flips of marked arrangements of pseudolines, and for rhombic tilings of a $2m$-gon; this answers an open question on flip graphs of pseudoline arrangements (SODA 2024). The reduction is from Vertex Cover: for every graph $G$ we construct two wiring diagrams at braid-move distance $|D|+2\operatorname{VC}(G)$, where $\operatorname{VC}(G)$ is the vertex cover number of $G$ and the Hamming distance $|D|$ is the number of triples of wires whose triangles are oriented differently. The construction glues copies of a seven-wire gadget whose braid-move distance exceeds its Hamming distance by $2$. Adding a line at infinity transfers the construction to rank-$3$ uniform oriented matroids, where two oriented matroids are adjacent in the mutation graph if their chirotopes differ in one basis; so deciding distance in the mutation graph is NP-complete in rank $3$. An iterate of Rambau's expansion of signotopes amplifies the excess and gives NP-hardness in every fixed rank $r\ge4$, and by duality in every fixed corank at least $3$. The same instances show that flip distance in the higher Bruhat orders $B(n,k)$ is NP-complete for every fixed $k\ge2$.

item.title: Continual Graph Memory and Community Infrastructure for AI-Assisted Mathematical Discovery
item.dc:creator: Eric Hanchen Jiang, Junyi Zhang, Jinxi Yu, Jiachen Lu, Zhi Zhang, Michael Simon, Justin Baker, Richard Cai, Sneha Agarwal, Yubei Li, Hyunsik Chae, Xinjie He, Kyle Zheng, Vigyan Sahai, Ethan Ji, Alexander K Taylor, Yiwen Kou, Kyle Hess, Xiao Liang, Yingnian Wu, J. D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, Andrea Bertozzi, Kai-Wei Chang, Eunice Jun, Raghu Meka, Nanyun Peng, Amit Sahai, Matthew Sottile, Terence Tao, Wei Wang
item.description:
The Ansätze platform integrates a fixed-interface Lean checker for proposed proofs, covering placeholders, allowed axioms and statement fidelity; five results have reported Lean formalizations.
Mathematical discovery requires preserving partial ideas and the evidence supporting their reuse. We present Ansatz, a research harness whose continual graph memory separates model-accepted claims and dependencies from curated exploration, and Ansatze, a community platform for inspecting, guiding and checking this work. On First Proof, Ansatz recorded nine local verifier closures in each of two ten-problem batches; a partial result in the Second Batch also counted as a pass under the study's criterion. These model-assessed outcomes include continued searches and differ from expert validation. Component studies and re-review expose disagreements and their dependency reach. Open-problem investigations produced candidate results, with five Lean formalizations reported. The platform connects problem discovery, research records, manuscript analysis and formal checking while preserving distinct evidence states. Together, these systems support cumulative human-AI research through persistent investigation and inspectable contributions.

item.title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
item.dc:creator: Dominic W. Berry, Abhishek Rawat, Sophia Simon, Guang Hao Low
item.description:
Accompanying Lean/Mathlib package (sparse-quantum-lean) formalizes the circuit constructions and query/gate bounds, with an appendix documenting conditional coverage.
We give quantum algorithms for time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations and linear systems, all with complexity that has only square-root dependence on matrix sparsity. Our algorithms retain optimal scaling in other relevant parameters such as time, condition number and precision. For several cases we prove matching lower bounds on the joint parameters and show that the additional gate overhead is only polylogarithmic in the inverse precision. The common primitive connecting our algorithms is the Cayley transform, which provides a cheap unitary embedding of the sparse matrices. For Hamiltonian simulation and differential equations, we then use transducers to construct the desired evolution operators. For linear systems, we instead encode the solution in the kernel of a matrix and use the Cayley transform to construct a projector onto that kernel.

item.title: Minimax Quantum State Tomography with Periodic Clifford Measurements
item.dc:creator: Hongru Zhao
item.description:
All labeled theoretical results, including minimax upper and lower bounds for quantum state tomography, are formalized in Lean, with code on GitHub and Zenodo.
Quantum state tomography provides a foundation for characterizing state preparation and predicting measurement outcomes. We characterize the minimax expected trace norm risk of quantum state tomography over classes with polynomial spectral decay under randomized nonadaptive single copy measurements. Under an explicit sufficient block size condition for the two layer periodic Clifford ensemble, we establish statewise expected trace norm oracle inequalities for operator norm minimum distance and measurement weighted projected least squares, with bounds that depend on each state's actual spectral tail, while the estimators require no prior knowledge of the state's structural characteristics, including its rank, eigenbasis, or spectral structure. Over these polynomial spectral decay classes, both estimators attain the minimax expected trace norm rates up to constants. As a direct consequence, the same estimators attain the minimax rate over every fixed rank constrained class, while remaining adaptive to the unknown structural characteristics of the state. For admissible logarithmic block sizes, the periodic Clifford measurements attain these guarantees with logarithmic elementary gate depth. The main technical ingredient is a uniform bound on the fourth moment of projectors for the periodic Clifford ensemble. The bound is sharp in dimension and holds for arbitrary test states, including those entangled across blocks. Covariance concentration and positivity yield adaptive oracle bounds, while a shared rotation information argument on spectral tail packings establishes matching lower bounds. We also provide polynomial time reconstruction algorithms, numerical comparisons, and Lean formalizations of all labeled theoretical results.

item.title: A Full Complexity Dichotomy for Complex-Valued Boolean Holant Problems
item.dc:creator: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng, Juqiu Wang
item.description:
The authors report completing a Lean formalization of the complexity dichotomy proof for Boolean Holant problems, with AI assistance.
A Boolean Holant problem evaluates a graph partition function specified by local signatures at its vertices. We prove a complexity dichotomy for arbitrary finite sets of algebraic complex-valued signatures on general graphs: an explicit, decidable criterion characterizes the polynomial-time cases, and every remaining case is $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. The proof resolves the all-even case by constructing signatures with nonzero endpoints and all remaining support on the central layer, then classifying them according to half their arity. Binary transfer groups and matching-product reconstruction provide the main tools in the small- and large-height cases, respectively.

item.title: Competitive Random-Order Correlation k-Clustering
item.dc:creator: Mahsa Derakhshan, Andisheh Ghasemi, Rajmohan Rajaraman, Omer Wasim, Tegan Wilson
item.description:
All theorems on correlation k-clustering approximation and competitive ratios are formalized in Lean, with proofs generated using Aristotle and Claude and hand-checked statements.
Correlation clustering has been extensively studied over the last two decades in many different computational models owing to its wide-ranging practical applications. The goal is to compute a partition of the vertex set such that the total number of disagreements, i.e. the sum of edges between clusters, and non-edges within clusters, is minimized. In this paper, we study correlation $k$-clustering, in which the total number of clusters is restricted to $k$. Correlation $k$-clustering is NP-hard, and while previous work has presented a polynomial time approximation scheme for constant $k$, there are no known results for general $k$. Our first result is a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithm for correlation $k$-clustering for general $k$. The main focus of this work is in the more challenging online setting. Noting that the best competitive ratio under adversarial arrivals is known to be $Ω(n)$, we concentrate on the well-studied random-order model, where vertices arrive in random order and on arrival of a vertex, edges to its earlier-arrived neighbors are revealed. We prove a surprising lower bound of $Ω(\log k)$-competitiveness for any online algorithm, which can be extended to $Ω(\log n)$ when $k = \text{poly}(n)$. Finally, the main result of this paper is a polylogarithmic upper bound on the competitive ratio for correlation $k$-clustering, using an algorithm inspired by the classic Pivot algorithm for correlation clustering. All theorems have been verified using Lean.

item.title: An $n^2\log\log n$ Lower Bound for Permanent Circuits with Valid Division
item.dc:creator: Jizhou Guo
item.description:
Rebuilds a third-party OpenAI Lean 4/Mathlib development and restates twelve of its declarations, checking types and axioms, to derive a permanent slice.
We record lower bounds for permanent circuits with valid division over characteristic zero, counting nonscalar multiplications and divisions while additions and scalar operations are free. Chapter 5 of OpenAI's Ten Advances supplies the block construction and critical-locus estimate; these, with the parameter choice made here and the classical bounds of Strassen and Baur-Strassen, give liminf as n tends to infinity of L_div(per_n)/(n^2 log_2 log_2 n) >= 1/12. Our finite-parameter refinement for matching-minor polynomials observes that the coefficient vector at deletion size h lies in a space of dimension at most min{binom(t,h), binom(t,d-h)}. Twelve machine-checked declarations of the Lean development accompanying OpenAI's manuscript on border determinantal complexity of the permanent (September 24, 2026) imply, by a short written argument, the existence of a geometric slice; a further written, unformalized application of the same criterion gives L_div(per_n) >= (n^2/119790) log_2(n/44) for n >= 1936. Assuming Proposition 7.3 of that manuscript gives the bound (n^2/86400) log_2(n/48) for n >= 1408. These are order-of-growth results; the elementary Hessian bound n^2/2 is larger at practical orders.

item.title: Continuity of Regularized Channel Rényi Divergences
item.dc:creator: Jinzhao Wang, Yuxiang Yang
item.description:
The main continuity theorem for regularized channel Rényi divergences is formalized in Lean, with the statement checked by Comparator and proofs replayed in the kernel.
We prove that the regularized, stabilized sandwiched Rényi divergence of finite-dimensional quantum channels converges to their regularized relative entropy as the Rényi order tends to one. The key tool is the channel hockey-stick divergence: Gour's Stinespring approximation bound and a Schatten norm estimate amplify an asymptotic bound below one into exponential decay at higher threshold rates. For channel pairs with finite max-relative entropy, known operational connections then give exponential strong converses for parallel and adaptive discrimination, a sharp zero–one testing law, and the subchannel asymptotic equipartition property.

item.title: A Szemerédi-Trotter Theorem in Arbitrary Fields
item.dc:creator: Mark Lewko
item.description:
The four explicit-constant incidence bounds of the main Szemerédi–Trotter theorem over arbitrary fields are formalized in Lean, with a public repository.
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p\ge0$. We prove that $m$ points and $n$ lines in $k^2$ determine at most $3(mn)^{2/3}+m+n+2mn/p$ incidences, the last term being omitted in characteristic zero. Over the prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ the coefficient of $mn/p$ can be replaced by $1$. The proof uses the polynomial method, and for $m=n$ the bound is sharp up to an absolute constant over prime fields. As applications, over prime fields in which $-1$ is not a square we obtain the $L^2\to L^r$ extension estimate for the paraboloid in $\mathbb{F}_p^3$ for $r>10/3$. Over every odd prime field, we show that a two-source extractor construction of Bourgain has exponentially small error at every min-entropy rate greater than $1/3$. We also improve sum-product estimates for small sets in positive characteristic and obtain projection and Furstenberg estimates over prime fields. The incidence inequalities with exact constants have been formalized in Lean.

item.title: Explicit channels with unbounded gains in classical communication using entangled inputs
item.dc:creator: Hao-Chung Cheng, Benjamin Lovitz, Peixue Wu
item.description:
All mathematical proofs of the explicit channel construction and its entropy bounds are formally verified in Lean, with a companion Lean verification artifact.
A seminal result of Hastings showed that entangled inputs can increase the rate of classical communication through independent uses of a quantum channel. While Hastings' result proved the existence of this phenomenon, it has remained a major open problem to find an explicit channel with this property. In this work, we resolve this question by constructing an explicit family of finite-dimensional quantum channels for which entangling inputs between pairs of channel uses yields an unbounded separation from the achievable communication rate using unentangled inputs. We describe a circuit implementation of our channel that uses only deterministic qudit Clifford unitaries and a single binary measurement with classical feedforward. The key ingredient is a careful design of the measurement and feedforward process that yields the required one-copy and two-copy output entropy bounds from moment estimates alone, without requiring strong convergence of the underlying unitary family.

item.title: The Zygmund conjecture and Rey's exponential integrability conjecture
item.dc:creator: Henri Martikainen
item.description:
The main results, including the continuous Zygmund estimate and sparse overlap bounds, are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib-only restatements and kernel plus Nanoda checking.
We prove the Zygmund conjecture in all parameters: the maximal operator associated with products of cubes with side lengths $(s_1,\ldots,s_{m-1},φ(s_1,\ldots,s_{m-1}))$, where $φ$ is any positive coordinatewise nondecreasing function, satisfies the weak $L(\log L)^{m-2}$ estimate for every $m\geq3$. The estimate is new for $m>3$. Our approach is to prove Rey's recent conjecture on the exponential integrability of the overlap function $h_{\mathcal G}=\sum_{I\in\mathcal G}\mathbf{1}_I$, with exponent $1/(m-1)$, for sparse incomparable families $\mathcal G$ of $m$-parameter dyadic rectangles, $m\geq2$. The Zygmund conjecture, even in the continuous form above, follows by strengthening a reduction given by Rey.

item.title: Lyapunov stability of polynomial vector fields is undecidable
item.dc:creator: Milan Korda
item.description:
The Main Theorem, undecidability of Lyapunov stability for homogeneous polynomial vector fields, is formalized in Lean, with the formalization produced by AI models.
We show that there are integers $N$ and odd $D$ such that no algorithm can decide, from the rational coefficients of a homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ in dimension $N$ of degree $D$, whether the origin is Lyapunov stable for $\dot Y=F(Y)$. This proves a conjecture of V. I. Arnold. We provide a Lean formalization of the proof. The smallest dimension $N$ for which we were able to prove undecidability is $N = 5$. An analogous undecidability result holds for global asymptotic stability and global exponential stability for non-homogenous vector fields. For dimension $N=2$ and homogenous vector fields, we establish decidability for all commonly used stability notions, building heavily on existing results.

item.title: Unbounded Holevo additivity gaps in finite dimensions
item.dc:creator: Jinzhao Wang
item.description:
The paper's results and proofs were autoformalized in Lean by an AI system and checked with the Comparator tool, and are released as a Lean certificate.
We establish unbounded two-use Holevo additivity gaps in finite dimensions. For each sufficiently large fixed integer $K$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we construct channels $T_n$ with output dimension $K^n$, input dimension $\exp(Θ_K(n^2))$, and \[ χ(T_n^{\otimes2})-2χ(T_n) \ge n\left[\frac{\log_2K}{K}-2\log_2(1+9/K)\right]-O(1/n). \] The gap is linear in output qubits, with an explicit quadratic input-qubit cost and an explicit threshold on $n$. We also obtain channels whose single-use Holevo quantity tends to zero while their two-use Holevo information, and hence classical capacity, diverges. The channels arise from structured tensor products of the complementary mixed-unitary channels used in Collins's free-probabilistic proof. We establish minimum-output-entropy gaps by combining Collins–Youn's product-group Haagerup inequality with Bordenave–Collins's quantitative strong-convergence estimates. We also provide a Lean certificate for our proofs.

item.title: Mahler's Problem on Liouville Numbers I. Analytic Rigidity
item.dc:creator: Diego Marques
item.description:
Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, the analytic rigidity results answering Mahler's question, are formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4; the code is in a public GitHub repository.
In 1984, Mahler asked whether a transcendental entire function can map the set of Liouville numbers $\mathscr{L}$ into itself. We answer this question in the negative by proving a local rigidity theorem for real-analytic functions. More precisely, if $U\subset\mathbb{R}$ is an open interval and $f:U\to\mathbb{R}$ is real-analytic with $f(\mathscr{L}\cap U)\subseteq\mathscr{L}$, then $f$ is the restriction to $U$ of a rational function in $\mathbb{R}(x)$. Quantitatively, there exists an absolute constant $τ>2$ such that, for every nonrational real-analytic function $f$ and every nonempty open subinterval $V\subset U$, the set of $ξ\in V\cap\mathscr{L}$ satisfying $μ(f(ξ))\leqτ$ contains a Cantor set. The proof combines a two-height counting estimate near analytic graphs with a nested-interval construction.

item.title: Partial Stabilizer Learning under Fixed Commuting Constraints and the Absence of a Copy-Rate Discount
item.dc:creator: Masahito Hayashi, Yimin Lu
item.description:
The main theorem on copy-rate thresholds for partial stabilizer learning is formalized in Lean 4, with source and verification records in a public repository.
We consider an unknown pure stabilizer state of \(n\) qudits with a fixed prime local dimension \(p\), together with prescribed commuting Pauli observables. Rather than learning the whole state, the learner must recover only complementary stabilizers that commute with the prescribed observables, together with their eigenvalues. Once the prescribed measurement is performed, this information and the observed outcome determine the corresponding conditional stabilizer state. We compare the number \(k\) of copies available to the learner with the number \(n\) of qudits and refer to their ratio \(k/n\) as the copy rate. Suppose that the dimension \(m\) of the requested complementary stabilizer subspace satisfies \(m=βn+o(n)\) for a fixed \(0<β\leq1\). If the copy rate converges to a value below one, the optimal exact recovery probabilities and verification scores converge to zero, both in the worst case and under the uniform prior. Conversely, if the number \(k\) of copies minus the number \(n\) of qudits tends to positive infinity, the entire stabilizer state can be identified with probability tending to one, and the requested complementary information can then be extracted. Thus, restricting the learning target to the stabilizer information needed after the prescribed measurement yields no copy-rate discount.

item.title: A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture
item.dc:creator: Hu Tan, Ying Zhang
item.description:
Lean code accompanying the finite-case verifications of the proof is released in a public GitHub repository.
Fraenkel's conjecture asserts that a partition of the integers into at least three Beatty sequences with distinct moduli has the binary densities $1,2,4,\ldots,2^{m-1}$, normalized by $2^m-1$. We prove the conjecture through a dimension-free intermediate statement: every such partition contains a component of density at least 1/3. After reducing the partition to primitive common-period data, Fourier cancellation produces a finite inverse-sine system. We prove that no such system can exist when every density is below 1/3. The proof combines a divisor-concentration identity with uniform analytic estimates and three exact finite verifications, all carried out with integer or rational arithmetic. The component supplied by the density bound has mean spacing at most three. Deleting it preserves balance, and every surviving periodic balanced set is again a rational Beatty set. Induction determines the surviving binary scales, while a two-sequence disjointness criterion forces the deleted density to be the next binary scale. This yields the asserted density pattern.An eventual Beatty representation of balanced binary indicators extends the classification to one-sided balanced sequences on at least three letters with distinct positive densities, proving the balanced-sequence conjecture of Altman, Gaujal, and Hordijk.

item.title: The circular law for non-Hermitian random band matrices: optimal bandwidth, periodic profile and discrete law
item.dc:creator: Yi Han
item.description:
A companion Lean 4/Mathlib formalization, publicly available on GitHub, checks the proofs of all four main circular-law theorems, apart from explicitly stated imported axioms.
We consider non-Hermitian random band matrices with growing bandwidth and study convergence of their empirical spectral distributions to the circular law. Let $N$ denote the matrix size and $W_N$ the bandwidth. From a universality perspective, it is conjectured that the circular law holds whenever $W_N\to\infty$. Previous results have mainly required $W_N\gg N^{1/2}$, with the principal exception of \cite{Han2511}, which proves the $W_N\to\infty$ circular law for an open-boundary block-tridiagonal model. Here we prove the circular law at this optimal threshold for several periodic models and under the near-optimal condition $W_N\gg\log N$ for a genuinely discrete model. For the periodic hard-indicator profile and its uniform and polynomially tapered generalizations, we prove the circular law under bounded-density and finite-third-moment assumptions whenever $W_N\to\infty$. At the same threshold, we prove the circular law for continuous, integrable profiles locally bounded below on every finite interval, including exponentially and Gaussian decaying profiles, with circular complex Gaussian entries. For the periodic full-block model, we prove the circular law under bounded-density and finite-third-moment assumptions whenever $W_N\to\infty$. The finite-third-moment assumption in the bounded-density results can be weakened to a finite $(2+α)$-moment assumption. For the same full-block model without a density assumption, we prove the circular law for centered variance-one real subgaussian atoms when $W_N\gg\log N$. The proof uses compositions of random transfer operators. An established high-band circular-law input on a short auxiliary ring calibrates the full exterior coefficient norm, and a boundary-uniform local comparison lifts this calibration to target rings even when $N/W_N$ is arbitrarily large.

item.title: Bounded Relative Boundary Implies Narrow DNF Approximation
item.dc:creator: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng
item.description:
The authors, with AI assistance, completed a Lean formalization of their proofs of the main DNF approximation theorem and Friedgut's conjecture.
We prove Friedgut's conjecture (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 12 (1999)) that every increasing family in the $p$-biased discrete cube with bounded relative boundary can be approximated arbitrarily well by one whose minimal elements have size bounded independently of the dimension and the bias. For $0<p\le 1/2$, every increasing Boolean function with total resampling influence at most $K$ is $\varepsilon$-close under $μ_p^n$ to a monotone DNF of width $\exp(O((K+1)^2/\varepsilon^2))$, from which the full conjecture follows for all $p\in(0,1)$. We build on Hatami's pseudo-junta theorem (Ann. of Math. 176 (2012)), whose approximator need not be increasing. Our randomized shifts produce an increasing approximator that is measurable with respect to a controlled refinement of Hatami's adaptive partition. Retaining only short positive certificates yields the desired narrow DNF.

item.title: A Dichotomy for Complex Boolean Holant with Binary Disequality
item.dc:creator: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng
item.description:
The full dichotomy proof is formalized in Lean, with public statements, proofs, exact certificates, and a Comparator-based challenge file; corrections were verified in Lean.
We classify Boolean Holant problems with a supplied binary disequality signature and an arbitrary fixed finite set of algebraic complex-valued signatures. Each problem is polynomial-time computable or $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard, and the tractability criterion is decidable. The proof combines arity reduction with the growth of the available binary transfer group and uses stable pairs to recover the structure of higher-arity signatures. We also prove a dichotomy for the disequality-edge model when the signature set contains an endpoint-nondegenerate irreducible eight-vertex signature, resolving the corresponding arity-four cases in the main proof.

item.title: Three omitted values and non-Blaschke point divisors in half-planes
item.dc:creator: Quanyu Tang, Bokai Cui, Wei He, Tao Hu, Yanyang Li, Ke Wang, Zijun Yu
item.description:
The main theorem, a counterexample to Nevanlinna's half-plane problem, is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib using Codex and checked by multiple independent kernels.
We construct a real meromorphic function $F$ on $\mathbb C$ such that $F^{-1}(\{0,1,\infty\})\subset\mathbb R$, while $F$ is not of bounded type in either half-plane. More strongly, for every $a\in\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}$, the $a$-point divisor in either half-plane fails the Blaschke condition. Thus the construction gives a negative answer to the half-plane bounded-type question arising from Nevanlinna's 1925 work. Postcomposition gives the analogous counterexample for any prescribed triple of distinct values in the Riemann sphere. The core construction and proof were generated during an autonomous run of GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra.

item.title: An explicit refined Gan–Gross–Prasad identity for Fourier–Jacobi periods of degree 2 Siegel cusp forms
item.dc:creator: Biplab Paul, Ameya Pitale, Abhishek Saha, Ralf Schmidt
item.description:
Local integral computations from Section 2 (Macdonald formula evaluations) are formalized and machine-verified in Lean 4, with a public GitHub repository.
We compute the local integrals appearing in the refined Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture for Fourier–Jacobi periods of $\mathrm{Sp}_4$ in new ramified cases and use this to formulate an explicit conjectural identity relating Petersson norms of degree 2 Siegel cusp forms and associated half-integral weight forms. We note consequences of our identity for the growth of Petersson norms, the size of Fourier coefficients, and non-vanishing of central $L$-values.

item.title: A proof of the 3-Decomposition Conjecture
item.dc:creator: Jicheng Ma
item.description:
The paper's results, including the proof of the 3-Decomposition Conjecture, are fully formalized in Lean 4, with a public GitHub repository.
We prove the 3-Decomposition Conjecture: every finite connected cubic loopless multigraph decomposes into a spanning tree, a 2-regular subgraph, and a matching. The proof rests on a new theorem on matching complements in subcubic graphs. Let H be a finite connected bridgeless simple graph of maximum degree three, and let S be its set of degree-two vertices, with |S| = k >= 2. We show that H has a matching of size equal to its cyclomatic number, |E(H)| - |V(H)| + 1, whose deletion leaves a single tree containing all of S, together with cycles disjoint from S. The proof is by induction on k.

item.title: Pattern-Derived Visual Swarm Games: Multi-Scale Drone-Vision States for Interception and Sustainability Audits
item.dc:creator: Faruk Alpay, Levent Sarioglu
item.description:
Ancillary Lean (and Coq) files check the finite encoder-selection inequality and fixed-point 128-by-128 numeric gain identities behind one result.
We convert drone-vision annotation streams into virtual swarm-game states without controlling physical drones. VisDrone and UAVSwarm metadata are compressed into a Bloom representation; deterministic probes produce bounded capability vectors, image-space formations, finite zero-sum payoffs, and human-readable visual overlays. The audit scales from $6\times 6$ to $32\times 32$ finite games and adds a repeated Markov layer with stock, fatigue, adaptation, exposure, stress, budget, data-growth, model-improvement, and entropy-budget state variables. Local screen tuning raises robust screen security from $0.526$ to $0.593$, and the $32\times 32$ tuned screen reaches value $0.616$. A field readout audit shows that fixed-pixel rasters do not improve monotonically: $128\times 128$ accuracy is $67.2\%$ and hotspot error is $0.136$. The diagnosed error is shrinking image-plane bandwidth. A finite empirical-risk encoder over scale-normalized Gaussian bandwidths selects a scale-normalized encoder with $λ=1.50$, reaching $77.6\%$ accuracy at $128\times 128$ and reducing joint loss by $0.185$. A server-side audit checks $16{,}777{,}216$ target-localization states, and a 32-round repeated-game audit over $16{,}777{,}216$ trajectories selects a budget-adaptive policy with value $0.461$.

item.title: Agenra: A Language and Verified Core for Stateful LLM Agent Authorization
item.dc:creator: Basavesh Ammanaghatta Shivakumar, Swarn Priya, Peng Gao
item.description:
Implements the agent authorization monitor as a compiled Lean core with proofs of client preservation under policy revisions, and Lean-checked simulation certificates for finite-quota revisions.
Applications that deploy LLM agents keep revising the permissions their agents use. When authority is consumable, even widening a permission can break a legitimate workflow, because an early call may use up a grant that a later call needs. Checking individual requests, or watching one run succeed, misses this. We present Agenra, a policy language with a Lean enforcement core that tracks the values each call uses, resources discovered at run time, and authority consumed by earlier calls. Agenra treats safety and workflow preservation as separate properties. Our key idea is to certify a revision with a simulation between the old and new permission ledgers. Quota increases, appended grants and independent reorderings admit such simulations by construction, and Lean checks proposed simulations for other finite-quota revisions. The proofs use the deployed matching predicates and extend through the full monitor, covering discovered resources, payloads that are never enumerated, failed calls and approvals. They assume serialized calls and identical service results under both policies, and they trust the Python translation layer. On 51 authored revisions, the checks certify all 21 that preserve their clients and none of the 30 that do not, and every lost workflow is confirmed by replay. They also certify a real quota increase from an open-source agent application. In a report-delivery application, raising the send quota preserves every client yet permits a second approved send, so preservation does not imply safety.

item.title: The Exceedance Design Effect: Effective Sample Size for Thresholds under Clustering
item.dc:creator: Adam Noonan
item.description:
The paper's central limit theorem, propositions, finite-sample counterexample and variance-estimator consistency are machine-checked in a 59-file Lean 4 and Mathlib proof bundle.
Suppose we want a cutoff that 90% of a population falls below. We estimate it from a sample, and another sample would give a different cutoff and a different fraction below it. We ask how much that fraction varies when observations come in independent groups, such as pupils in classrooms or sentences in news articles. We prove that grouping multiplies its large-sample variance by $1+(m-1)ρ_I(p)$, where $m$ is the group size, $p$ is the target fraction, and $ρ_I(p)$ measures whether two members of a group fall on the same side of the cutoff. That correlation can differ from the correlation between the scores themselves, and it changes with the target. We give a direct proof, a counterexample to using score correlation, and an extension to unequal group sizes. A dataset therefore does not have one effective sample size. How much information it contains depends on the question you ask. In our document experiment, the same 1,000 rows carried about 217 independent observations' worth of information at the median. At the 95th percentile, they carried about 621. Nothing about the dataset changed. We asked it a different question. The number of rows is a property of the dataset. The effective sample size belongs to the analysis.

item.title: Polynomial growth of complex polynomial Bohnenblust–Hille constants
item.dc:creator: Daniel M. Pellegrino, Eduardo V. Teixeira
item.description:
The paper's results and proofs are reported as formalized in Lean 4 using Lea, a formalization system from the authors' DARPA ExpMath project.
For complex \(m\)-homogeneous polynomials, let \(D_m\) denote the optimal dimension-free constant in the polynomial Bohnenblust–Hille inequality. We prove that, for every \(B>1/2\), there exists \(K_B>0\) such that \[ D_m\le K_B m^B,\qquad m\ge1. \] More precisely, we obtain the square-root-scale estimate \[ D_m\le \sqrt m\,\exp\!\bigl(C\sqrt{\log m}\,\log\log m\bigr). \] The proof combines coefficient-preserving degree reduction with a weighted bootstrap, separating balanced and dominant degree profiles. We also determine the critical linear-dimensional asymptotics: \[ D_{m,n_m}\longrightarrow 2 \qquad\text{whenever}\qquad \frac{n_m}{m}\longrightarrow1, \] and consequently \(\liminf_{m\to\infty}D_m\ge2\). Further applications give two-sided bounds for homogeneous Sidon constants and a quantitative logarithmic remainder in the multidimensional Bohr-radius asymptotic.

item.title: Isometric embeddings of trees: why 32 leaves can require six dimensions, and bounds for every tree
item.dc:creator: Logan R. Chalmers
item.description:
Both main theorems, the 32-leaf six-dimension obstruction and the universal 1.162832 log2 t upper bound, are formalised in Lean with proofs archived on Zenodo.
We identify the first failure of the $\lceil\log_2 t\rceil$ leaf-count bound for isometric embeddings of $t$-leaf trees under the maximum norm. Every tree with at most $31$ leaves attains the bound, but a $32$-leaf tree requires six dimensions. This answers a question of Fitzpatrick and Nowakowski and disproves a conjecture of Aksoy, Kılıç and Koçak. We explain this failure by showing how requirements within and between branches force an additional coordinate. For a family of three-branch trees, we prove that the leaf bound is attained exactly when the two larger branches have equal leaf counts; otherwise, one additional coordinate is necessary. We also prove that every tree embeds in $\lceil 1.162832\log_2 t\rceil$ dimensions, improving the coefficient of approximately $1.44042$ established in 2005. These results hold for arbitrary positive edge lengths and the entire metric realization. We also construct infinite families in which the excess persists under repeated leaf expansion. Both main theorems are formalised in Lean using only standard axioms.

item.title: From Block Orthogonality to Decidability in Complex-Weighted Counting CSP
item.dc:creator: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng
item.description:
The authors formalized the decidability and structural proofs in Lean; during formalization they found a gap in a corollary of Young's isomorphism theorem and repaired it.
In a landmark JACM paper recognized with the 2021 Gödel Prize, Cai and Chen established a complexity dichotomy for counting CSPs over arbitrary finite domains with algebraic complex weights. Their tractability criterion consists of three conditions on the infinite family of functions obtained from CSP instances by summing out some variables: the Block Orthogonality and Type Partition conditions, and a Mal'tsev polymorphism condition on support and row-equivalence relations. They left open whether this criterion is decidable from the finite set of constraint functions. We resolve this question by giving a total exact algorithm for every $q$-element domain ($q\ge 1$), with algebraic weights encoded exactly. We also prove that the Block Orthogonality condition implies the other two conditions, reducing the tractability criterion to a single structural property. We obtain similar decidability and structural results for Lin's tractability criterion for $\#\mathrm{CSP}^{d}$, where each variable occurs a multiple of $d$ times. Our method first shows that every failure of Block Orthogonality can be witnessed by a generated function of arity at most $q^2+1$. At each such arity, we reduce checking infinitely many generated functions to finitely many exact algebraic tests, using tensor products and a pinned extension of Young's all-instance isomorphism theorem. For the structural implication, we use powers of generated functions to control complex cancellation and construct functions whose supports encode row equivalence. These constructions yield the Type Partition and Mal'tsev polymorphism conditions.

item.title: A Human Audit of OpenAIs AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs
item.dc:creator: Mikołaj Sienicki, Krzysztof Sienicki
item.description:
Audits OpenAI's AI-generated proofs, which come with public Lean 4 certificates, examining the repository snapshot, sorry counts, and how Lean statements correspond to the published theorems.
We assess 18 chapter-specific reviews of the ten mathematical results announced by OpenAI on 1 August 2026, alongside review standards, Lean formalizations, subsequent research, and mathematical references. The article audits this review record without claiming a complete reconstruction of all ten proofs.
